role: customer-facing product help source; contains no proprietary implementation details

features.title: Scientific Canvas
features.what_you_see: A visual workspace where modules can be placed, moved, connected, grouped, and inspected.
what_it_looks_for: Valid typed connections between visible ports
features.rigor: Canvas layout is presentation only. Scientific meaning comes from the connected module contracts and executed verification, not from where a node is drawn.
examples: Create a small experiment by adding a data/source module, a transformation module, and a result/check module; connect only ports that the UI accepts.
Duplicate an experiment, change one visible parameter, run both, and compare outputs and verification states without changing the module topology.

features.title: Module Library
features.what_you_see: Searchable scientific, mathematical, verification, research, and utility modules.
what_it_looks_for: A scientific task or data type
A module whose visible inputs/outputs match that task
features.rigor: Each module exposes a visible contract: accepted inputs, produced outputs, parameters, maturity, and evidence categories. Hidden implementation is not required to use the contract correctly.
examples: Search for a module by category, inspect its visible inputs and outputs, then drag it onto the canvas.
Compare two modules that produce the same public output type and choose one based on maturity, assumptions, and verification needs.

features.title: Typed Connections
features.what_you_see: Ports connect only when their public data types and declared unit contracts are compatible.
what_it_looks_for: Matching declared units when units are present
features.rigor: Connections fail closed on incompatible public contracts. A successful connection means the data interface is compatible; it does not by itself prove that the chosen scientific workflow is meaningful.
examples: Connect an output labeled as the same public type as a downstream input; the UI accepts the edge when the contract matches.
Try connecting ports with incompatible declared units; CACE rejects the edge instead of silently converting or guessing.

features.title: Parameters and Units
features.what_you_see: Editable module parameters with visible type/default/unit metadata.
what_it_looks_for: Values of the expected public type
Exact declared unit convention where applicable
features.rigor: Parameters are validated at execution boundaries. Declared unit contracts are exact and explicit rather than silently converted.
examples: Run a module with its default visible parameters, then repeat with one parameter changed and compare the evidence panel.
Enter values using the module's declared unit convention; if a connected module declares a different unit contract, insert an explicit conversion module rather than relying on an implicit conversion.

features.title: Experiment Execution
features.what_you_see: Run controls, progress, outputs, and per-module results.
features.rigor: The runtime validates the graph before execution and keeps execution separate from verification. A run completing does not automatically mean the result is verified.
examples: Run a three-module graph and inspect which nodes executed and what outputs were produced.
Intentionally leave a required input disconnected and observe that validation fails before scientific execution begins.

features.title: Verification and Evidence
features.what_you_see: PASS, FAIL, NOT_RUN/stale-style result states and evidence categories attached to executed checks.
what_it_looks_for: The verifier's explicit conditions and evidence type
features.rigor: Evidence categories are kept separate. Missing or skipped verification is never presented as success, and a numerical result is never silently promoted to formal proof.
examples: Run an experiment whose checker passes and inspect the evidence type rather than relying only on the green status.
Disable or make an optional backend unavailable and confirm the result shows NOT_RUN/unavailable rather than PASS.

features.title: Proof Explorer
features.what_you_see: Read-only views of claim status, hypotheses, evidence ceiling, and whether current source is formally qualified.
features.rigor: Formal status is controlled separately from ordinary module execution. Customer help describes scope and assumptions but does not expose theorem bodies or proprietary formalization details.
examples: Open a formally supported result and inspect its visible assumptions and current qualification state before using it in a report.
Open a conditional claim and verify that the condition remains visible rather than being hidden by a successful numerical experiment.

features.title: Save, Replay, and Export
features.what_you_see: Experiment files, run reports, replay/fingerprint tools, and customer-safe exports.
features.rigor: Saved experiments preserve public semantic structure separately from presentation state. Provenance/fingerprints identify content but do not create mathematical truth.
examples: Save an experiment, reopen it later, rerun it with the same seed/settings, and compare the replay report.
Export a customer-safe report showing module names, visible inputs/outputs, parameters, results, and evidence labels without source implementation details.

features.title: 2D / 3D Visualization
features.what_you_see: Switchable 2D and 3D views, pan/zoom, and rotatable scientific visualizations.
features.rigor: View transforms do not change scientific semantics unless the user explicitly adds a scientific transformation module.
examples: Inspect the same result in 2D and 3D and confirm the underlying experiment/evidence state does not change.
Rotate a 3D view to inspect structure from another angle, then reset the camera without rerunning the experiment.

features.title: Coordinate and Tiling Views
features.what_you_see: Cartesian and alternative tiling/coordinate visualizations such as square, triangular, hexagonal, hierarchical, or other supported layouts.
what_it_looks_for: Data that can be visualized spatially
features.rigor: Coordinate/tiling presentation is visually informative but cannot alter proof/evidence unless represented by an explicit scientific transform in the graph.
examples: View the same point/field data on Cartesian and hexagonal presentation grids and compare visual structure.
Use a hierarchical/fractal-style address view for navigation while keeping the experiment graph and verification state unchanged.

features.title: Research Ideas and Build on Canvas
features.what_you_see: Editable research idea cards with hypotheses, proposed experiments, associated modules, evidence notes, and lifecycle status.
features.rigor: Idea status is research workflow metadata, not proof. Proposed graphs are previewed before being added to the scientific canvas.
examples: Create an idea, associate two relevant modules, generate a Minimal proposal, preview it, and then add it to the canvas.
Compare Minimal, Balanced, and Exploratory proposed graphs for the same idea and choose one based on compute cost and testability.

features.title: Local AI Assistant
features.what_you_see: Optional local-model assistant for explanation, research suggestions, and experiment planning.
features.rigor: AI output is advisory only and never becomes scientific evidence or formal proof. High-capability/network permissions are independently gated.
examples: Ask the local AI to explain what a selected module expects and receive a customer-safe explanation without changing the experiment.
Ask for three experiment ideas, review them, and manually approve only the one you want to place on the canvas.

features.title: Conway Heartbeat
features.what_you_see: Activity/attention state that connects canvas modules, AI attention, and resource/economy views.
features.rigor: Heartbeat state is orchestration metadata only. It cannot make a result verified or alter mathematical truth.
examples: Run an experiment and observe heartbeat activity move through nodes that changed or executed.
Use Protein Play or Open Problem Play to raise research attention on selected objects while keeping their scientific evidence unchanged.

features.title: Spare-Compute Economy
features.what_you_see: Internal non-monetary compute credits, resource headroom, task bids, and scheduling outcomes.
features.rigor: The scheduler uses measurable resource/task information, while verification remains separate. AI self-reports cannot create rewards or evidence.
examples: Let two research tasks bid for limited spare compute and inspect which one is scheduled first.
Compare two strategies over repeated host-measured runs and use the measured efficiency history for future scheduling.

features.title: Math Coin Research Economy
features.what_you_see: A simulated fixed-supply compute-right economy layered above internal scheduling credits.
features.rigor: Economic state is completely separate from scientific truth. Any production real-asset integration requires separate security/compliance review.
examples: Simulate a compute purchase where a bounded amount of MATH is reserved and burned only after measured compute settlement.
Model a decade vault release event and observe market/resource effects without changing any scientific result or proof status.

features.title: Open Problems Toolkit
features.what_you_see: Source-backed cards for open scientific/mathematical problems that can be imported to the canvas and explored.
features.rigor: Problem status is date-stamped research metadata. AI or numerical exploration cannot mark an open problem solved.
examples: Import a sourced open problem card to the canvas and ask Local AI for decompositions, invariants, and computational tests.
Filter the catalog by field/status, choose a problem, and build a small exploratory graph without changing the problem's official status.

features.title: Protein Playground
features.what_you_see: Imported protein structure outputs, residue-level inspection, provenance/confidence information, and heartbeat Play.
features.rigor: Protein Play is read-only research analysis. Imported predictions remain predictions and do not become experimental/clinical evidence.
examples: Select an imported protein and run Play to highlight residues with interesting confidence/contact patterns for further inspection.
Compare two protein structures from separate runs while preserving each one's source, license, attribution, and evidence limitations.

features.title: AlphaFold DB Import
features.what_you_see: A UniProt accession field and attributed AlphaFold DB import into a typed protein object.
what_it_looks_for: Network permission for the import broker
features.rigor: Retrieval preserves public source/license/attribution and content identity. CACE does not reproduce AlphaFold or claim the prediction is experimentally proven.
examples: Enter a UniProt accession, import the available structure, inspect attribution, then open it in Protein Playground.
Import two proteins by accession and compare their visible structures/confidence while keeping source records separate.

features.title: Atoms, Molecules, and Chemistry Experiments
features.what_you_see: Typed atom/molecule objects and chemistry experiment modules suitable for safe computational/home-lab planning.
what_it_looks_for: A module appropriate to the intended experiment
features.rigor: CACE keeps computed/predicted properties distinct from measured observations and displays limitations/evidence type.
examples: Create or import a simple molecule object, connect it to a property-analysis module, and inspect the evidence label on the result.
Build a comparison experiment for two candidate molecules using the same visible conditions and compare predicted properties without treating them as measured facts.

features.title: Materials Search
features.what_you_see: Search/generation workflows for candidate materials and predicted property screens.
features.rigor: Generated candidates are hypotheses. Property predictions retain their evidence class and require separate experimental validation where appropriate.
examples: Specify a target set of public properties, generate candidate materials, and rank them by the visible predicted outputs.
Take one candidate and pass it through two independent property-analysis modules, then compare their evidence/limitations before deciding whether to test it experimentally.

features.title: Physics Objects
features.what_you_see: Draggable typed physics objects such as fields/particles/other supported conceptual objects and related experiment modules.
features.rigor: The canvas object is a typed scientific representation. Visual presence alone does not imply a physical claim; executed modules and evidence determine result status.
examples: Place two compatible physics objects on the canvas and connect them through an analysis module with matching typed ports.
Compare the same input object under two different public parameter settings and inspect which conclusions are numerical, symbolic, interval, or formal.

features.title: Accounts and Profiles
features.what_you_see: Account/profile settings including user type, optional declared location scope, protein-library consent, and local-AI Math Coin wallet identity.
features.rigor: Profile/economic data never changes scientific evidence. Sensitive wallet material is not stored in ordinary profile fields.
examples: Create a Researcher profile with region-level declared location and protein-library storage enabled.
Create a Basic profile without location disclosure or protein storage and use CACE normally with those features disabled.

features.title: Local AI Economy Pairing
features.what_you_see: Network OFF/ON, distinct Receive and Outgoing connection codes, code-entry fields, and linked-instance status.
what_it_looks_for: A valid peer code for the intended direction
features.rigor: Codes are directional, short-lived, and single-use. Pairing grants only narrow economy/heartbeat capabilities and not shell/filesystem/proof/wallet-key authority.
examples: Enable networking on two instances, enter instance B's Receive code into A's outgoing connection field, and establish A→B only.
Create the reverse B→A relationship separately with a second explicit pairing rather than assuming bidirectional trust.

features.title: Account Protein Library
features.what_you_see: Optional saved protein objects associated with an account.
what_it_looks_for: A typed protein object with provenance
features.rigor: Storage preserves source/license/attribution metadata and is separate from verification/proof.
examples: Enable protein storage, import an attributed protein, and save it to your account library for later experiments.
Keep storage disabled and verify that imported proteins remain session/experiment data rather than being persisted to the account library.

features.title: Payments and Canonical Monero Receive Wallet
features.what_you_see: Customer-facing payment/quote/invoice state where enabled; private wallet custody stays behind the server boundary.
features.rigor: Payment state is commercial metadata and never scientific evidence. Browser/AI never receives wallet private keys.
examples: Display a server-generated invoice/receive request using the configured canonical CACE wallet infrastructure.
Confirm a payment/licensing event changes commercial access state only, leaving all scientific verification states untouched.

features.title: CACE Build Lite
features.what_you_see: A compact JSON build/test plan for coding agents and developers.
features.rigor: Build Lite uses deterministic dependency/critical-path/cache scheduling and has no scientific/proof authority.
examples: Run Build Lite after changing web files and execute only the cheap impacted checks before a broader regression.
Run the proof profile after formal-source changes and observe that proof-sensitive cache hits remain restore-only rather than skipping qualification work.

features.title: Customer Help Center
features.what_you_see: Searchable feature/module help with safe examples, visible contracts, connection suggestions, and rigor explanations.
features.rigor: Help content is generated from a strict allowlist and leakage policy. It explains public behavior and rigor boundaries without exposing proprietary implementation or custom mathematics.
examples: Open a module help page before using it and review its required inputs, outputs, parameters, evidence labels, and two sample experiments.
Search for a workflow goal, open two compatible module pages, and use the suggested connection examples as a starting point while still checking scientific appropriateness.
